li.a: Human Rights Watch: Response to Armenian Government Letter on the town of Khojaly, Nagorno-Karabakh (23 March 1997)
Anadolu Agency: 'Perpetrators of Khojaly genocide should be punished' (25 February 2021)
Anadolu Agency: Victims massacred in 1992 by Armenian forces in Azerbaijani town Khojaly remembered in Ankara (26 February 2024)
1news.az: Khojaly Tragedy: Events, International Testimonies, and Informational Breakthrough (25 February 2026)
Armenian National Committee of Australia: The Khojaly Genocide Fabrication
EJIL: Talk!: Armenia v Azerbaijan before the European Court of Human Rights (1 October 2020)

content.p: On the night of 25 to 26 February 1992, with the Soviet Union barely dissolved, Karabakh Armenian forces took the town of Khojaly in Nagorno-Karabakh. Hundreds of Azerbaijani civilians were killed, wounded or captured, many of them while trying to flee the town. Azerbaijan says 613 people died and calls the event genocide. Human Rights Watch, which investigated it in 1992, held Karabakh Armenian forces directly responsible for the civilian deaths. Armenian officials and advocacy groups reject that account. The Armenian foreign ministry said in 1997 that Azerbaijani militia blocked and shot at civilians who tried to leave, and the Armenian National Committee of Australia says Azerbaijani forces fired on the fleeing column.

No page consulted for this account reports an international court ruling that settles the question. What exists is a set of competing documents: a human rights investigation, official casualty lists, an Armenian counter-narrative and, decades on, a yearly ritual of remembrance.

By the start of 1992, according to the Azerbaijani commentary published by 1news.az, Khojaly was under a de facto blockade. It mattered because it held the only airport in the region. The same account says the town was shelled repeatedly in February 1992 while armed formations gathered around Askeran and Khankendi, then called Stepanakert.

The Armenian National Committee of Australia, an advocacy group (called the committee below), tells the story from the other side. It says Azerbaijani special militia units had shelled Armenian civilian targets with rockets through 1991 and early 1992, and that the blockade of the airport left Stepanakert short of food, fuel and medicine. In its telling, Armenian forces had to silence the fire coming from Khojaly and end the blockade. It adds that the Armenians saw an Azerbaijani move on Askeran, and then on the capital, as coming. These are the group's claims; the pages consulted do not confirm them.

The committee describes Khojaly's inhabitants as mostly Meskhetian Turks who had been settled there in Soviet times, and says the population was 2,000 to 2,500. Another point is drawn from Azerbaijani sources: 1news.az reports that the 366th Guards Motorized Rifle Regiment of the former Soviet Army, based in Khankendi, played a role in the fighting. It quotes what it describes as a classified report by a Colonel V. Savelyev. According to that quotation, the regiment's commander and others joined Armenian forces in operations toward Khojaly, and the report numbers the Azerbaijanis shot in the squares at 49 and the Azerbaijanis killed during the withdrawal of the population at 58. These figures come second hand, through a Baku-based outlet, and are not an independent count.

Human Rights Watch and the Armenian-side group both say the town's people were told an attack was coming. HRW's letter says its 1992 report found that many residents may have had advance warning, because an ultimatum had been handed by Armenian forces to the militia chief of Khojaly at that time, Alif Gajiyev, who passed the warning to civilians. HRW added that Karabakh Armenian officials and fighters clearly expected the inhabitants to flee, since they claimed to have told the town that a corridor would be left open for safe passage.

The committee says loudspeakers carried the announcements for ten days and that the corridor led to Azerbaijani-held areas. It says the Azerbaijani authorities did nothing to help people leave. It also cites the former mayor of Khojaly, who it says told a Moscow newspaper that he had asked for helicopters to evacuate residents and received no help.

The committee says Armenian forces attacked at 11:30 p.m. on 25 February, and that the operation lasted three and a half hours. Anadolu Agency, citing Azerbaijani figures, describes a two-hour offensive and writes that Armenian forces took the town on 26 February after battering it with heavy artillery and tanks, helped by infantry. The two accounts differ on duration and on how the operation is characterised, and neither is a neutral record of the hour-by-hour events.

The account that matters most for the civilians is the one about the flight. The Helsinki Watch report of 1992, as described in HRW's 1997 letter, and the work of the Moscow-based Memorial Human Rights Center, found that the retreating Azerbaijani militia fled Khojaly alongside some of the large groups of fleeing civilians. Helsinki Watch noted that by remaining armed and in uniform the militia could be considered combatants, and that they therefore endangered the civilians, even if their intent had been to protect them.

The same report, quoted in the letter, states that an attacking party must still take precautions to avoid or limit civilian casualties and must suspend an attack that may be expected to cause excessive civilian losses. It says the circumstances of the attack on the people fleeing Khojaly indicated that Karabakh Armenian forces and troops of the 366th CIS regiment deliberately disregarded this restraint. Since Karabakh officials and fighters expected the inhabitants to flee, it argued, the killing of fleeing combatants could not justify the foreseeably large number of civilian casualties.

Azerbaijani authorities give 613 killed, among them 106 women, 63 children and 70 elderly people. Anadolu Agency, reporting those figures in 2021 and again in 2024, adds 487 seriously injured and 1,275 Azerbaijanis captured, about 150 of whom it says remain missing. It also states that eight families were wiped out entirely, that 130 children lost one parent and that 25 lost both. The 1news.az piece, written by Namik Aliyev, who describes himself as a member of the Azerbaijani parliamentary commission on the crimes, gives the toll as 631 rather than 613 while repeating the other categories, including 76 injured children. The pages do not explain the difference. This account follows the 613 given by Anadolu and by the Azerbaijani statements it cites.

A lower early figure comes from a Helsinki Watch report of September 1992, as quoted by 1news.az. It cites Namig Aliyev, head of a department of the Azerbaijani parliament and a member of the group investigating Khojaly, as telling Helsinki Watch in April 1992 that 213 Khojaly victims had been buried in Agdam. Some of those brought to a temporary hospital there were identified as military personnel, he said, and many of the men had no documents, so they could not be classed as military or civilian. He also reported that 33 of the bodies examined had been scalped, had parts missing or were otherwise mutilated.

The committee argues the figure has grown over time. It says Azerbaijani sources first reported about 100 casualties, then 1,234 a week later, and that in 1992 two Azerbaijani journalists gave Memorial a helicopter video which, it says, showed fewer than 60 civilian casualties. It also says Armenian forces reported 11 Azerbaijani civilian casualties and handed all civilians to the Azerbaijani authorities. It also says, citing the Republic of Armenia, that mutilation of bodies took place near Agdam, on territory held by Azerbaijani forces. None of these claims is supported by the other accounts consulted here.

The Armenian argument was set out in an official statement that HRW answered in March 1997. Armenia's foreign ministry said that the Azerbaijani Popular Front militia had prevented the civilians from leaving through the passes Karabakh Armenians had left open, and that the militia shot people who tried to flee. It cited a 1992 Helsinki Watch report and an interview with the former Azerbaijani president Ayaz Mutalibov in support.

HRW's executive director replied that the ministry had misrepresented the organisation's findings. Neither its own report nor Memorial's, the letter said, contained any evidence that Azerbaijani forces obstructed the civilians' flight or fired on them. It still placed direct responsibility with Karabakh Armenian forces. The letter also corrected two other figures the ministry had attributed to HRW: the 1988 pogrom in Sumgait, which HRW's report says took the lives of 32 Armenians, and the estimate of ethnic Armenians who fled Azerbaijan, which HRW put at 300,000 to 350,000, not 600,000.

The committee offers further Armenian-side material. It quotes Mutalibov, after he resigned, as saying that according to Khojaly inhabitants who escaped, the events had been organised to remove him and that he did not believe Armenians would grant a safe corridor and then shoot at escaping civilians. It also cites Azerbaijani figures, among them the human rights activist Arif Yunusof, who wrote in July 1992 that the town and its citizens were deliberately sacrificed to a political goal, and Tamerlan Karaev, who is quoted as saying the tragedy was committed by Azerbaijani authorities. These statements are the group's selection and are not corroborated by the other pages consulted. Anadolu Agency and the Azerbaijani commentary, meanwhile, present Armenian forces as the perpetrators and describe the event as genocide.

The 1news.az piece adds a quotation from the Armenian historian and diplomat Jirair Libaridian, who in 1992 was chief adviser to Armenia's first president, Levon Ter-Petrosyan. The piece quotes his 2014 article as saying that writing about Khojaly is hard for an Armenian, because "something unacceptable" was done there, and it links that to civilians being mutilated and killed by Armenian forces in Karabakh. The wording here paraphrases the piece and is not a direct quotation.
content.h2: Law, memory and the long aftermath
content.p: The European Court of Human Rights has not judged Khojaly in any case described by the pages consulted. An analysis in EJIL: Talk! notes that the court's earlier judgment in Chiragov and others v Armenia confirmed that Armenia had effective control of Nagorno-Karabakh and the territories around it, and that more than a thousand similar individual applications from people displaced from Karabakh around 1992 were then pending.

Azerbaijan has pressed for an international legal assessment of Khojaly as genocide. The 1news.az piece says dozens of countries have recognised it as such and claims Azerbaijan itself has convicted a first group of war criminals, without naming the cases. Anadolu Agency, in 2021, reported the head of the World Azerbaijani Congress, Asif Kurban, as saying fifteen parliaments and sixteen US state assemblies had recognised the genocide and calling for the perpetrators to be punished. He said Armenia bore responsibility because it had effective control over those who carried out the actions. The committee calls the genocide charge a propaganda campaign by Baku.

The anniversary is marked every 26 February. In 2024, the thirty-second anniversary, Anadolu Agency reported a ceremony at the Khojaly Memorial Museum in Ankara, where Azerbaijan's ambassador said the largest Khojaly memorial in Turkey stands, and a ceremony in Sarajevo. The same year's coverage notes that the Karabakh region had returned to full Azerbaijani sovereignty the previous autumn. 1news.az calls Khojaly a symbol of national grief in Azerbaijan, while the competing accounts above remain unreconciled.
